hints: Think about what type of chemical can pull a proton off the ammonium ion to free ammonia gas.
Remember that $\text{NH}_4^+$ acts as a weak acid, so it needs a strong base like hydroxide ions and gentle warming to release $\text{NH}_3$.
Check which of the four reagents is basic and can supply $\text{OH}^-$ to react with $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$ on heating.
walkthrough:
**Spot the ammonium ion chemistry**

Think of $\text{NH}_4^+$ as $\text{NH}_3$ holding an extra $\text{H}^+$. To liberate $\text{NH}_3$, you need a base to remove that $\text{H}^+$.

General rule:
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Apply it to ammonium sulfate**

Ammonium sulfate, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$, warmed with a soluble hydroxide gives ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus blue.

Reaction with calcium hydroxide:
$$(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4 + 2\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Choose the basic reagent**

Only aqueous calcium hydroxide, $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, provides $\text{OH}^-$ ions. The other reagents are oxidising agents or acids, so they cannot deprotonate $\text{NH}_4^+$ to give $\text{NH}_3$.

options.A: Aqueous bromine, $\text{Br}_2$, is an oxidising agent, not a base. It does not supply $\text{OH}^-$ to deprotonate $\text{NH}_4^+$, so no ammonia is liberated.
options.B: Dilute hydrochloric acid, $\text{HCl}$, adds $\text{H}^+$ and keeps nitrogen as $\text{NH}_4^+$. An acid cannot convert ammonium into ammonia, the reverse reaction is favoured.
options.C: Aqueous calcium hydroxide provides $\text{OH}^-$ ions which react with $\text{NH}_4^+$ on warming to give $\text{NH}_3$ and water. This is the classic test for ammonium salts.
options.D: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is a strong oxidising agent used to test for reducing agents. It is acidic, not basic, so it will not liberate $\text{NH}_3$ from an ammonium salt.
